issues.title: Incorrect parameter for getCallerReward might return 0 reward despite insolvency
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/markets/bigBang/BigBang.sol#L577


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The calculation of the caller reward uses an incorrect value. If the exchangeRate remains the same but a lot of interest accrues, then there will be no liquidation reward. Without a liquidation reward borrowing positions will not get liquidated and incur bad debt for the protocol.

## Proof of Concept
The function `Market._getCallerReward` is called in `BigBang._liquidateUser` like this:

```js
//BigBang
uint256 callerReward = _getCallerReward(
    userBorrowPart[user],
    startTVLInAsset,
    maxTVLInAsset
);

//Market
    function _getCallerReward(
        uint256 borrowed,
        uint256 startTVLInAsset,
        uint256 maxTVLInAsset
    ) internal view returns (uint256) {
        if (borrowed == 0) return 0;
        if (startTVLInAsset == 0) return 0;

        if (borrowed < startTVLInAsset) return 0;
```

The issue is that `userBorrowPart` does not describe the actual borrowed value/debt, but just his share of the total debt. The part does not increase over time through accruals (opposed to the elastic value which the part describes). 

A simple example:
- user provides 1 ETH collateral at a current price of 2000$
- with a collateralization rate of 75% the user can borrow up to 1500$
- he borrows 1499$. assuming no interest has accrued yet, his `userBorrowPart` will also be 1499 (ignoring 1e18 factor for simplicity).
- now interest accrues and users actual debt will increase. He is insolvent at 1500, but in the code above `if (borrowed < startTVLInAsset) return 0` will always be true, because  `borrowed` will always be 1499 (`startTVLInAsset` is point of insolvency, here 1500).

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Use the elastic value (users debt consisting of borrowed amount + interest)


## Assessed type

Other

issues.title: borrowInternal() of BaseTOFTMarketModule.sol has phantom permit functions
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/master/contracts/tOFT/modules/BaseTOFTMarketModule.sol#L293-#L303


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

A malicious actor could steal funds from a User who has already done his first deposit. 

## Proof of Concept

Consider the case where attacker uses a token with phantom permit function as collateral, the most famous ones being WETH, BNB, HEX etc. Let’s consider WETH in this example.  
Attack Scenario: 
Attacker calls borrowInternal() of BaseTOFTMarketModule.sol, with carefully inputted `approvals` parameters to skip the first 2 “if” conditions of `_callApproval` function. 
Subsequently, performing IERC20Permit(approvals[i].target).permit() functionality with Attacker inputted variables where attacker inputs approvals[i].owner to an account who has already deposited some tokens through the functionality in order 
BaseTOFTMarketModule.sol:borrowInternal()->MagnetarMarketModule.sol: _depositAddCollateralAndBorrowFromMarket -> MagnetarMarketModule.sol: _extractTokens  
 
Thereby confirming Users approval of the token for the MagnetarMarketModule.sol 
 
3) As Weth doesn’t have a permit function , permit() call will get directed to it’ fallback  
function. Weth has a fallback functionality as below:  
```solidity  
 
function() public payable { 
 
deposit(); 
 
} 
 
 
function deposit() public payable { 
 
balanceOf[msg.sender] += msg.value; 
 
Deposit(msg.sender, msg.value); 
 
} 

 
```  
This function is called when receiving ETH (and just deposits it, to mint wrapped ETH with it) but, crucially, is also called when an undefined function is invoked on the WETH contract. All WETH of all such users can be stolen and deposited onBehalf of the Attacker. 
 
Another Vulnerability of the Tokens with Phantom Permits: 
Unexpected reverts are caused by IERC20Permit(approvals[i].target).permit() by tokens like stETH which does not have a permit function.

Manual Review

issues.title: Re-entrancy in flash minting USDO can bypass max checks
Setting debtStartPoint > 0 breaks many BigBang actions
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/markets/bigBang/BigBang.sol#L192


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
If `BigBang.debtStartPoint` is set to a value > 0, many core features will break, e.g. deposits of collateral will be possible, but removal not, which would effectively lock collateral inside the contract.

## Proof of Concept
`BigBang.getDebtRate` uses the variable `debtStartPoint` to offset the starting point where interest begins to rise:

```js
uint256 debtPercentage = ((_currentDebt - debtStartPoint) *
    DEBT_PRECISION) / (_maxDebtPoint - debtStartPoint); 
```

`debtStartPoint`, which is only set once during `init`, would be greater than `_currentDebt` after initialization and cause an underflow. All actions that depend on `getDebtRate` would be unusable, These actions are: 
borrow, repay, buyCollateral, sellCollateral, liquidate, and removeCollateral. Adding collateral is however still possible, making it possible for collateral to get locked.

This has not been discovered during testing as all tests currently set `debtStartPoint` to 0:

```js
bigBangRegData = await registerBigBangMarket(
    mediumRiskBigBangMC.address,
    yieldBox,
    bar,
    wbtc,
    wbtcAssetId,
    usd0WethOracle,
    ethers.utils.parseEther('1'),
    ethers.utils.parseEther('0.5'),
    ethers.utils.parseEther('0.005'),
    ethers.utils.parseEther('0.035'),
    0, // -> debtStartPoint
    staging,
);
```
## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

The following check is missing: `if (_currentDebt < debtStartPoint) return minDebtRate;`





## Assessed type

Other

## Impact
All the ETH in `(m)TapiocaOFT` can be stolen, which is relevant when the underlying asset `erc` is ETH.

## Proof of Concept
`(m)TapiocaOFT` allows removing collateral from `Singularity` through a cross chain call, but the address of the `MarketHelper` is not validated. 

To send a cross chain `removeCollateral()` transaction, users call `removeCollateral()` of `BaseTOFT` (which is inherited by `(m)TapiocaOFT`), and calls `_lzSend()` internally. 

Then, the LayerZero endpoint calls `lzReceive()` in the destination chain of `(m)TapiocaOFT`, which eventually reaches `_nonBlockingLzReceive()`. Here, the `packetType` is `PT_MARKET_REMOVE_COLLATERAL` and the function `remove()` from the `BaseOFTMarketModule` is called.

Then, it calls `withdrawToChain()` of address `removeParams.marketHelper`, without checking its validity, with a `msg.value` of `withdrawParams.withdrawLzFeeAmount`. Thus, a malicious market can be sent as `removeParams.marketHelper` and a `withdrawParams.withdrawLzFeeAmount` of the eth balance of the `(m)TapiocaOFT` contract. issues.title: Reentrancy vulnerability in SGLLendingCommon._removeCollateral
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/master/contracts/markets/singularity/SGLLendingCommon.sol#L41-L55


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
This vulnerability could allow an attacker to withdraw collateral from the SGLLendingCommon contract without actually removing it. This could result in a loss of funds for the lender.

## Proof of Concept
The SGLLendingCommon._removeCollateral function is vulnerable to reentrancy attacks. Reentrancy occurs when a contract calls another contract, and the second contract calls back to the first contract before the first contract has finished executing. This can allow the first contract to be tricked into performing unintended actions.

In the case of SGLLendingCommon._removeCollateral, the function calls the yieldBox.transfer function. The yieldBox.transfer function can call back to the SGLLendingCommon contract if the user of the yieldBox has also deposited collateral in the SGLLendingCommon contract. This could allow the user to withdraw their collateral from the SGLLendingCommon contract without actually removing it, which would effectively double-spend their collateral.

The following is a proof of concept for the vulnerability:

The attacker deposits collateral into the SGLLendingCommon contract.
The attacker calls the SGLLendingCommon._removeCollateral function, passing in the address of the yieldBox contract.
The yieldBox.transfer function calls back to the SGLLendingCommon contract.
The attacker withdraws the collateral from the SGLLendingCommon contract.
The SGLLendingCommon contract does not remove the collateral from the attacker's account.

## Tools Used
VScode
## Recommended Mitigation Steps
The following are recommended mitigation steps for this vulnerability:

The yieldBox.transfer function should be modified to not allow callbacks to the SGLLendingCommon contract.
The SGLLendingCommon contract should implement a reentrancy guard.
The SGLLendingCommon contract could use a timelock.

issues.title: `exitPosition` in `TapiocaOptionBroker` may incorrectly inflate position weights
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token-audit/blob/59749be5bc2286f0bdbf59d7ddc258ddafd49a9f/contracts/options/TapiocaOptionBroker.sol#L316


# Vulnerability details

### Impact
Users who `participate()` and place stakes with large magnitudes may have their weight removed prematurely from `pool.cumulative`, hence causing the weight logic of participation to be wrong. `pool.cumulative` will have an incomplete image of the actual pool hence allowing future users to have divergent power when they should not. In particular, this occurs during the `exitPosition()` function.

### Proof of Concept 
This vulnerability stems from `exitPosition()` using the current `pool.AverageMagnitude` instead of the respective magnitudes of the user's weights to update `pool.cumulative` on line 316. Hence, when users call `exitPosition()`, the amount that `pool.cumulative` is updated but may not be representative of the weight of the user's input.

Imagine if we have three users, Alice, Bob, and Charlie who all decide to call `participate()`. Alice calls `participate()` with a smaller amount and a smaller time, hence having a weight of 10. Bob calls `participate()` with a larger amount and a larger time, hence having a weight of 50. Charlie calls `participate()` with a weight of 20.
#### Scenario 

+ Alice calls `participate()` first at time 0 with the aforementioned amount and time. The `pool.cumulative` is now 10 and the `pool.AverageMagnitude` is 10 as well. Alice's position will expire at time 10.
+ Bob calls `participate()` at time 5. The `pool.cumulative` is now 10 + 50 = 60 and the `pool.AverageMagnitude` is 50.
+ Alice calls `exitPosition()` at time 10. `pool.cumulative` is 60, but `pool.AverageMagnitude` is still 50. Hence, `pool.cumulative` will be decreased by 50, even though the weight of Alice's input is 10.
+ Charlie calls `participate` with weight 20. Charlie will have divergent power in the pool with both Bob and Charlie, since 20 > `pool.cumulative` (10).

# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/master/contracts/markets/MarketERC20.sol#L251-L284


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

In `MarketERC20.sol` we have `_permit()` function:
```solidity
function _permit( /
        bool asset, // 1 = asset, 0 = collateral
        address owner,
        address spender,
        uint256 value,
        uint256 deadline,
        uint8 v,
        bytes32 r,
        bytes32 s
    ) internal {
        require(block.timestamp <= deadline, "ERC20Permit: expired deadline");

        bytes32 structHash = keccak256(
            abi.encode(
                asset ? _PERMIT_TYPEHASH : _PERMIT_TYPEHASH_BORROW,
                owner,
                spender,
                value,
                _useNonce(owner),
                deadline
            )
        );

        bytes32 hash = _hashTypedDataV4(structHash);

        address signer = ECDSA.recover(hash, v, r, s);
        require(signer == owner, "ERC20Permit: invalid signature");

        if (asset) {
            _approve(owner, spender, value);
        } else {
            _approveBorrow(owner, spender, value);
        }
    }
```

In this function, the signed data doesn't include the `chainId` and because of this cross-chain replay attacks are possible.
## Proof of Concept

According to [EIP4337](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4337) standard to prevent replay attacks the signature should depend on `chainId`. But in these functions, `chainId` is not used. 
A valid signature that was used on one chain could be copied by an attacker and propagated onto another chain.
## Tools Used

Manual review
## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Add `chainId`  `_permit()` function `structHash`.

```solidity
bytes32 structHash = keccak256(
            abi.encode(
                asset ? _PERMIT_TYPEHASH : _PERMIT_TYPEHASH_BORROW,
                owner,
                spender,

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
A malicious contract could: 
1.	Take a flash loan
2.	Call liquidate(), passing manipulated arrays to liquidate honest users
3.	Profit from bonuses
4.	Repay the flash loan


## Proof of Concept
The liquidate() function takes array parameters that specify which users to liquidate and how much to liquidate. There are no checks on the caller of liquidate() - any contract can call it.

A flash loan contract could manipulate the arrays passed into liquidate() to liquidate arbitrary users. For example, a malicious contract could take a flash loan, call liquidate() to liquidate honest users, profit from bonuses, and repay the flash loan.

There are no checks like: 
o	Ensuring the caller has skin in the game / collateral
o	Checking the caller is not a contract
o	Limiting liquidatable amounts per call


## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps 
Add a onlyEOA modifier to liquidate() to prevent contracts from calling it

Other

Within the getDebtRate() function of the contract, a vulnerability exists that could potentially hinder the operation of the contract. This vulnerability arises when _currentDebt falls below debtStartPoint, triggering an overflow in the computation of debtPercentage. As the getDebtRate() function is indirectly called in each important function (through ‘_accrue()’) such as borrow(), repay(), removeCollateral(), and liquidate(), this overflow issue could break the functionality of the contract.

The proof of concept is embedded in the contract code. In the getDebtRate() function, the calculation for debtPercentage is executed as follows:

This prevents the getDebtRate() function from returning a valid "protocol debt rate", which could cause the contract to revert on most of the contract’s function.

Manual Audit

## Impact

The `YieldBox` contract is going to be deployed on multiple chains ([confirmed in contest discord channel](https://discordapp.com/channels/810916927919620096/1125494082375000244/1131670307279745125)). Since `block.chainid` is not used anywhere in the signature, the functions `permit` and `permitAll` are vulnerable to cross chain replay attacks.

## Proof of Concept

A replay attack occurs when an attacker is able to copy a valid transaction involving another users signature, and send it to the network again. It is for this reason that nonces are used. However when the same contract exists on multiple chains, since the nonces are handled separately it is possible for a transaction on one chain to be replayed by attacker on another chain. For more info on cross chain replay attacks, see [this medium article](https://medium.com/coinmonks/what-the-heck-is-replay-protection-aae910f2a3cb). The fact that the `YieldBox` contract is intended to be deployed to potentially ["dozens of networks"](https://docs.tapioca.xyz/tapioca/) significantly increases the attack surface.

Consider the following example:
- Alice calls `permit` where owner=Alice and spender=Bob on mainnet, using the first nonce
- Bob calls `permit` where owner=Alice and spender=Bob and the same assetId and deadline as Alice's initial mainnet call, but on Arbitrum L2 instead
- The call will succeed, as the signatures will be identical (assuming Alice has not yet increased her nonce on Arbitrum)
- Bob has successfully allowed himself to spend Alice's tokens on Arbitrum, despite Alice only intending for Bob to spend her tokens on mainnet

Manual review

Implement `block.chaini

The `emergencyWithdraw` function in `LidoEthStrategy` uses a hardcoded `minAmount` value to define slippage tolerance when swapping using Curve's ETH/stETH pool. This value is intended to be 0.5% (inline comment), however it is written `(toWithdraw * 50) / 10_000` instead of `toWithdraw - (toWithdraw * 50) / 10_000`, which instead allows for 99.5% slippage. This provides essentially zero slippage protection and puts practically all of the funds being withdrawn at risk of MEV sandwich attacks. Since `emergencyWithdraw` always withdraws the strategy's entire balance, this puts all users funds at risk.

## Proof of Concept

```solidity
File: tapioca-yieldbox-strategies-audit\contracts\lido\LidoEthStrategy.sol

104:     function emergencyWithdraw() external onlyOwner returns (uint256 result) {

106: 
107:         uint256 toWithdraw = stEth.balanceOf(address(this));
108:         uint256 minAmount = (toWithdraw * 50) / 10_000; //0.5%  @audit incorrect calculation
109:         result = curveStEthPool.exchange(1, 0, toWithdraw, minAmount);
110: 
111:         INative(address(wrappedNative)).deposit{value: result}();
112:     }
```

    minAmount = (1000e18 * 50) / 10_000
              = 5e18
              = 5 ETH

The transaction would succeed even if the swap results in the contract receiving as little as 5 ETH from 1000 stETH input.

Manual review

Correct the calculation on line 108:

The `Vesting.registerUser` function is used to register a new user to the `Vesting` contract. Each of the vested amount for each new user is accumulated and cached into the `_totalAmount` state variable. After all the users are registered the `Vesting.init` function is called to initialize the contract.         if (_seededAmount == 0) revert NoTokens();
        if (_totalAmount > _seededAmount) revert NotEnough();

The issue here is that `_seededAmount > _totalAmount` scenario can occur thus passing the above `require` check.

Now let's consider the following scenario:

1. There are 3 users (A, B, C) who are registered in the vested contract.
2. Following are vested amounts for each of the users.
    A = 50
    B = 30
    C = 20

6. Let's assume all the users claim after the `duration` has passed.
7. They call the `Vesting.claim` function and receive their vested amounts (50, 30, 20) respectively.
8. Hence the `_totalClaimed` will be `100` now.
9. Once these respective users have claimed there is still a balance left in the contract as shown below:

# Vulnerability details


Oracle implementations `ARBTriCryptoOracle` and `SGOracle` for Singularity markets are using the deprecated Chainlink `latestAnswer()`. There are also no checks to ensure that the returned price value is valid and not stale.

This will affect the `updateExchangeRate()` function in Singularity, which uses the price returned from `latestAnswer()` to derive the collateral price.

The issue will affect the Singularity markets, where inaccurate collateral prices will cause `USDO` to be borrowed at a wrong exchange rate.

Use `latestRoundData` function instead and add checks to ensure the returned price is invalid and not stale.

Oracle

Miners or attackers can manipulate transaction order to incorrectly compute amounts.
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/markets/singularity/SGLLiquidation.sol#L37-L38


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
An attacker could exploit this by:
- Calling liquidate directly without first calling _accrue().
- The exchange rate will be stale, so liquidation amounts computed will be incorrect.
- The attacker profits from improper liquidation amounts.


## Proof of Concept
Calling _accrue updates the exchange rate and various balances. However, it is called after fetching the exchange rate.
 _accrue() accrues interest on borrow amounts before liquidation. This updates totalBorrow and userBorrowPart.Liquidation amounts depended on these updated balances from _accrue() however, _accrue() is called before amount calculations, not atomically with it. Miners or attackers could reorder transactions to call liquidate() before _accrue(). This would mean liquidations happen on stale data, not updated balances. As a result, liquidated amounts could be higher or lower than intended.


This means the exchange rate fetched on line 1 could be stale if another transaction calls _accrue in between. The computed amounts would be incorrect.
For example:

- Bob has 10 ETH collateral, 5 ETH borrow
- _accrue() should make his borrow now 5.5 ETH
- Liquidator tries to liquidate Bob's 5.5 ETH borrow
- But miner inserts liquidate call before _accrue()
- So liquidator repays only 5 ETH instead of intended 5.5 ETH


## Tools Used
Manual
## Recommended Mitigation Steps 
_accrue should be called first before fetching any state


## Assessed type

Other

# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-yieldbox-strategies-audit/blob/05ba7108a83c66dada98bc5bc75cf18004f2a49b/contracts/balancer/BalancerStrategy.sol#L138-L147


# Vulnerability details

### Impact

The BalancerStrategy uses a cached value to determine it's balance in pool for which it takes Single Sided Exposure.

This means that the Strategy has some BPT tokens, but to price them, it's calling `vault.queryExit` which simulates withdrawing the LP in a single sided manner.

Due to the single sided exposure, it's trivial to perform a Swap, that will change the internal balances of the pool, as a way to cause the Strategy to discount it's tokens.

By the same process, we can send more ETH as a way to inflate the value of the Strategy, which will then be cached.

Since `_currentBalance` is a view-function, the YieldBox will accept these inflated values without a way to dispute them

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-yieldbox-strategies-audit/blob/05ba7108a83c66dada98bc5bc75cf18004f2a49b/contracts/balancer/BalancerStrategy.sol#L138-L147

    function _deposited(uint256 amount) internal override nonReentrant {
        uint256 queued = wrappedNative.balanceOf(address(this));
        if (queued > depositThreshold) {
            _vaultDeposit(queued);
            emit AmountDeposited(queued);
        }
        emit AmountQueued(amount);

        updateCache(); /// @audit this is updated too late (TODO PROOF)
    }
```

- Imbalance the pool (Sandwich A)
- Update `updateCache`
- Deposit into YieldBox, YieldBox is using a `view` function, meaning it will use the manipulated strategy `_currentBalance`
- `_deposited` trigger an `updateCache`
- Rebalance the Pool (Sandwich B)
- Call `updateCache` again to bring back the rate to a higher value
- Withdraw at a gain

### Result

Imbalance Up -> Allows OverBorrowing and causes insolvency to the protocol
Imbalance Down -> Liquidate Borrowers unfairly at a profit to the liquidator

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/master/contracts/markets/singularity/SGLLendingCommon.sol#L76
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/master/contracts/markets/singularity/SGLLendingCommon.sol#L96


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
It is possible to borrow more than the limit established in the totalAsset control variable. This is only possible because in line 76 of the contract SGLLendingCommon.sol the number of shares to be borrowed is converted from uint256 to uint128. This occurs in the act of borrowing and repayment.

Two types of impacts are possible, reducing the value of the _totalAsset.elastic variable to a value that makes it unfeasible for users to take out borrows, or increasing the variable above what was established, can be scaled to a value so high that it does not allow repayments.

## Proof of Concept
Case 1:
- A user makes a loan of 340282366920938463463374607431768211456 (max uint128 + 1).
- On line 76, in the _borrow function, the value will change to zero after the conversion from uint256 to uint128, consequently not dexrementing the variable that controls the amount of assets (_totalAsset.elastic).
- The user repays the loan with an amount smaller than the largest number of uint128 and because the value does not cause overflow, the _totalAsset.elastic variable will be incremented. This will make the _totalAsset.elastic variable have a value greater than the initial one.
- If this value is increased to a value close to uint 256.max, users will be unable to repay their borrow.

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/master/contracts/usd0/modules/USDOLeverageModule.sol#L169
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/master/contracts/usd0/modules/USDOMarketModule.sol#L168
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/master/contracts/usd0/modules/USDOOptionsModule.sol#L174
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/master/contracts/tOFT/modules/BaseTOFTLeverageModule.sol#L184
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/master/contracts/tOFT/modules/BaseTOFTMarketModule.sol#L160
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/master/contracts/tOFT/modules/BaseTOFTOptionsModule.sol#L189
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/master/contracts/tOFT/modules/BaseTOFTStrategyModule.sol#L152


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The modules listed above expose public functions that accept an argument `address module` and delegate call to the `module` address. These modules are delegatecalled by the main contract, USDO or TOFT, with fixed arguments in `address module`. 

This design is a waste of gas, and more importantly, it’s not safe, because the delegatecall to an unknown address risks arbitrary code execution. 

If we start the transaction from USDO context, we cannot control the `address module`. If we invoke the vulnerable function on the module contract directly, only the meaningless storage of that module will be affected, the storage of the USDO contract cannot be modified and everything is safe. 

However, if the malicious contract does selfdestruct in the context of that module, the code of the module will be removed permanently. The main contract can no longer call any function in the dead contract. Even worse, Since the modules are hardcoded inside the non-upgradable USDO/TOFT contract, the bug will cause permanent DOS of this project. 

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Do not use `address module` as an argument in public functions. 


## Assessed type

call/

issues.title: attacker can drain asset in StargateStrategy
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-yieldbox-strategies-audit/blob/05ba7108a83c66dada98bc5bc75cf18004f2a49b/contracts/stargate/StargateStrategy.sol#L241


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept
The core attack is because `_currentBalance()` is manipulatable to be arbitrarily large. `_currentBalance()` uses `compoundAmount()` which swap reward token to wrappedNative using `swapper.buildSwapData()`. The attacker can pre-manipulate reward-wrappedNative pool such that reward price per wrappedNative is arbitrarily high using flash loan attack. Now the attacker can call `YieldBox.withdraw()` with `share == 0` and `amount` to be very large. The function will calculate `share` as `amount._toShares()` which will be extremely small because `_tokenBalanceOf(asset)` is extremely large and therefore pass the `_burn()` and is able to drain the asset from the strategy.

## Tools Used
manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use oracle prices for reward and wrappedNative to cross-check that `swapper.getOutputAmount()` returns manipulated price within a certain threshold.


## Assessed type

Oracle

issues.title: Exchange rates from Compound are assumed to have 18 decimals
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-yieldbox-strategies-audit/blob/master/contracts/compound/CompoundStrategy.sol#L115-#L116


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The CompoundStrategy.sol assumes the exchange rates (borrowing rate) of Compound always have 18 decimals,which is not true. According to the Compound documentation here (https://compound.finance/docs/ctokens#exchange-rate), the exchange rate returned from the exchangeRateStored function is scaled by 1 * 10^(18 - 8 + Underlying Token Decimals) . This could lead to significant Scaling issues in the Protocol’s calculations and logic.

## Proof of Concept

Let’s take an example of cETH. Let’s assume the exchange rate for cETH is 0.02 (which means one cETH is worth 0.02 ETH), then we need to divide it by 10 ^ (18 + 18 - 8) = 10 ^ 28 to get the actual amount of ETH that one cETH represents. In this case, it would be 0.02 / 10 ^ 28 = 2 * 10 ^ -30 ETH. 

But in case of Tapioca, it assumes the exchange rate to be of 18 decimals and thereby divides the value with 10**18 to get a wrong whole number as shown here - https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-yieldbox-strategies-audit/blob/master/contracts/compound/CompoundStrategy.sol#L115-#L116 

However, this would not be correct, because the exchange rate for cETH is not of 18 decimals. It is actually of 28 decimals, as we saw in the previous example. Therefore, multiplying it by 10 ^ 18 would result in a value that is off by a factor of 10 ^ (28 - 18) = 10 ^ 10. This could lead to significant errors and inconsistencies in the protocol’s calculations and logic. 


## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

To avoid this issue, the protocol should either use the exact exchange rate from Compound without any rounding or scaling, or use the correct formula to adjust for the difference in decimals between the cToken and the underlying asset. This way, the protocol can ensure that it is using accurate and compatible values for its opera

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Unexpected behaviour of smart contract leading to loss of funds.

The USDOLeverageModule.sol#multiHop function has branching with `if` statement that checks the value of the `success` return value from the `delegatecall`. The syntax is wrong that the transfer function on line 180 will never be executed because there is also a revert function in the if block.

        address module,
        uint16 _srcChainId,
        bytes memory _srcAddress,
        uint64 _nonce,
        bytes memory _payload
    ) public {
...//ommited code
if (!success) {
            if (balanceAfter - balanceBefore >= amount) {//@audit this should be outside the outer if.
                IERC20(address(this)).safeTransfer(leverageFor, amount);
            }
            revert(_getRevertMsg(reason)); //forward revert because it's handled by the main executor
        }

        emit ReceiveFromChain(_srcChainId, leverageFor, amount);
    }
```
## Tools Used
Manual Review.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Refactor if branch code to so that the second `if` statement is not nested in the the above `if` statement because the first if statement block will always revert.

issues.title: SGOracle exchangeRate is instantaneous and can be used for arbitrage
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph-audit/blob/023751a4e987cf7c203ab25d3abba58f7344f213/contracts/oracle/implementations/SGOracle.sol#L51


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The exchangeRate represents the exchange ratio of the internal accounting share. Generally speaking, it should only charge the borrow interest with time, and increase.
However, in SGOracle, chainlink oracle's latestAnswer is involved in the computation of exchangeRate, and although it can not be manipulated, it changes frequently, resulting in the computation of exchangeRate being instantaneous, rather than only increasing with the staking time and borrow.
This creates a space for sandwich arbitrage, in which arbitragurists listen to the mempool, clamp the tx of the oracle price updating, and make sandwich trades before and after the price update to achieve arbitrage.

## Proof of Concept

```solidity
    function _get() internal view returns (uint256 _maxPrice) {
        uint256 lpPrice = (SG_POOL.totalLiquidity() *
            uint256(UNDERLYING.latestAnswer())) / SG_POOL.totalSupply();

        return lpPrice;
    }
```

Assuming that latestAnswer changes from 1 to 1.2 and `totalLiquidity / totalSupply` remains unchanged, arbitrageurs can deposit funds and mint share when latestAnswer is 1, and then withdraw funds when latestAnswer rises. 
Because exchangeRate is instantaneous, this gives attackers the ability to run out of vault with ample funds.

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

ExchangeRate should not be computed using instantaneous values


## Assessed type

MEV

The function will calculate `share` as `amount._toShares()` which will be extremely small because `_tokenBalanceOf(asset)` is extremely large and therefore pass the `_burn()` and is able to drain the asset from the strategy. 

## Tools Used
manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Use oracle prices for reward and wrappedNative to cross-check that `swapper.getOutputAmount()` returns manipulated price within a certain threshold. 


## Assessed type

Oracle

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/bcf61f79464cfdc0484aa272f9f6e28d5de36a8f/contracts/tOFT/modules/BaseTOFTOptionsModule.sol#L221-L258

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

An option of USD0/TOFT can be seized by the attacker, if this option is exercised by its owner from a different chain. 

  

## Background 

`exerciseOption` function in `BaseUSDO.sol`/`BaseTOFT.sol` is the entry point of cross-chain option exercise. 

The function is called when 

1. A *user U* wants to exercise an *option O* (represented by an NFT) from a different chain. 

2. *option O* belongs to him on target chain B. 

3. He wants to pay for this option on *chain A* with some ONFT (USDO or TOFT). 

Suppose the *user U* owns an **100 TapiocaOFT - 1000 USDO** option, which allows him to exchange 100 TapiocaOFT for 1000 USDO. The user U exercises this option from chain A. 

`exerciseOption` of `BaseTOFT.sol` will: 

1. burn 100 TapiocaOFT of user U on chain A. 

2. send a cross-chain message to chain B's `TapiocaOFT.sol` via LayerZero. 

When the message arrives, `TapiocaOFT.sol` will exercise the option (`oTAPTokenID`) on behalf of User U. It will 

1. Mint 100 TapiocaOFT 

2. Exercise the option by calling `exerciseOption ( TapiocaOptionBroker.sol:351 )`. The `TapiocaOptionBroker.sol` will 

    1. Check if `msg.sender` (which is `TapiocaOFT.sol`) is permitted for the option. 

    2. Take 100 TapiocaOFT from `TapiocaOFT.sol` 

    3. Transfer 1000 USDO to `TapiocaOFT.sol`. 

3. Transfer 1000 USDO to the receiver specified in the cross-chain message. 

To exercise the option, `TapiocaOFT.sol` should be allowed to transfer the option NFT specified by `oTAPTokenID`. It could be approved in a separated transaction on chain B or in an embedded ERC721 permit signature that could be executed in the `_callApproval` function

## Impact
`BigBang.getDebtRate` might underflow, and the method is also used in the `_accrue` method, the accruing might not work as well.

## Proof of Concept
In `BigBang.getDebtRate`, when we get `debtPercentage` from `_currentDebt`, we validate the upper bound, but not for the lower bound. So the calculation might underflow when `_currentDebt` < `debtStartPoint`.

```solodity
        if (_currentDebt >= _maxDebtPoint) return maxDebtRate;

        uint256 debtPercentage = ((_currentDebt - debtStartPoint) * 
            DEBT_PRECISION) / (_maxDebtPoint - debtStartPoint);
```

## Tools Used
Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
We can add another validation for the lower bound.

```solidity
    if (_currentDebt <= debtStartPoint) return minDebtRate;
```

Under/Overflow

# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/usd0/USDO.sol#L81-L89


# Vulnerability details

Because `maxFlashLoan` doesn't change dynamically, it's possible to call `flashLoan` multiple times, sidestepping the `maxFlashMint`

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/usd0/USDO.sol#L81-L89
```solidity
    function flashLoan(
        IERC3156FlashBorrower receiver,
        address token,
        uint256 amount,
        bytes calldata data
    ) external override notPaused returns (bool) {
        require(token == address(this), "USDO: token not valid");
        require(maxFlashLoan(token) >= amount, "USDO: amount too big");
        require(amount > 0, "USDO: amount not valid");
```

The function `maxFlashLoan` always returns `maxFlashMint`, allowing it to sidestep the cap if calling the function more than once

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/usd0/USDO.sol#L57-L59
```solidity
    function maxFlashLoan(address) public view override returns (uint256) {
        return maxFlashMint;
    }
```

### POC
- Call flashLoan twice with `maxFlashMint`
- you now have twice the `maxFlashMint` and have sidestepped the max limit

### Mitigation

Consider computing `maxFlashMint` with a cap, based on `totalSupply`

For example `totalSupply > maxFlashMint ? 0 : maxFlashMint - totalSupply`

Invalid Validation

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
*Note* - Setting this to HIGH because the operator initiates the transaction with a customer as from. This means he doesn’t need to front run from he can front and back run his, the operator, own transaction. 

An operator can set specific parameters and sandwich transactions to unbalance the pool which can cause `collateralShare` to be set to zero which bypasses the `_allowedBorrow()` check leading to loss of funds for `from`.  An operator can do this by setting both `minAmountOut` and `borrowAmount` to zero and then manipulating the timing of transactions to unbalance and rebalance the pool. This leads to `collateralShare` being zero, effectively bypassing the `_allowedBorrow` check.

## Proof of Concept
1. The operator sets minAmountOut and borrowAmount to zero.
2. The operator sets supplyAmount to the desired amount.
3. The operator front-runs this transaction with another transaction to unbalance the pool.
4. When the swap occurs, collateralShare equals 0, which bypasses the _allowedBorrow check.
5. The operator back-runs this transaction with another transaction to rebalance the pool.

## Tools Used
manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add _allowedBorrow to line 345 to ensure that msg.sender is allowed to interact with from's account at supplyAmount.

MEV

issues.title: Operator can force customers to `addCollateral()` on his behalf
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/master/contracts/markets/bigBang/BigBang.sol#L288
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/master/contracts/markets/singularity/Singularity.sol#L235


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
The `allowedBorrow()` modifier on the `addCollateral()` checks if `msg.sender` is allowed to interact on `from`’s behalf via an `allowanceBorrow` mapping located in the `MarketERC20` contract. If so `_addCollateral()` is called. An if statement checks if `share` is zero if so it sets `share` to the value returned by the call to `yieldBox.toShare` where amount is used. 

An operator can set `share` to zero which passes the check in the `allowedBorrow()` modifier since 0 isn’t greater than 0. An operator can set `amount` to a number that doesn’t exceed the amount of collateral `from` has. When `_addCollateral()` sees that `share == 0` it will set `share` to the value returned from `yieldBox.toShare` using `amount` passed in by the operator. From here `share` is added to the operator’s address and then deducted from `from`. The operator can then withdraw this collateral via `removeCollateral()`. 

## Proof of Concept
Operator calls addCollateral setting `to` to an address he controls, from to a customer, amount to an amount from has, and share to zero. 

Operator bypasses the allowedBorrow modifier with share set to zero. 

In _addCollateral attackers share is adjusted by yieldBox.toShare using the amount the operator passed in 

Share is added to the operator 

Share is deducted from customer 

Operator then calls removeCollateral with share matching the share he just received 

Operator receives collateral 



## Tools Used
manual

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Remove amount variable. 

OR

Don’t allow share to be zero. 








## Assessed type

Other

```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/master/contracts/tOFT/BaseTOFT.sol#L99


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

This is an issue that affects all the contracts that inherit from `NonBlockingLzApp` due to incorrect overriding of the `lzSend` function and lack of input validation and the ability to specify whatever [`adapterParams`](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/master/contracts/tOFT/BaseTOFT.sol#L101) you want.
The consequence of this is that anyone can with a low cost and high frequency keep on blocking the pathway between any two chains, making the whole system unusable.

## Proof of Concept

#### Layer Zero minimum gas showcase

While sending messages through LayerZero, the sender can specify how much gas he is willing to give to the Relayer to deliver the payload to the destination chain. This configuration is specified in [relayer adapter params](https://layerzero.gitbook.io/docs/evm-guides/advanced/relayer-adapter-parameters).
All the invocations of `lzSend` inside the TapiocaDao contracts naively assume that it is not possible to specify less than 200k gas on the destination, but in reality, you can pass whatever you want.
As a showcase, I have set up a simple contract that implements the `NonBlockingLzApp` and sends only 30k gas which reverts on the destination chain resulting in `StoredPayload` and blocking of the message pathway between the two lzApps. 
The transaction below proves that if no minimum gas is enforced, an application that has the intention of using the `NonBlockingApp` can end up in a situation where there is a `StoredPayload` and the pathway is blocked.

Transaction Hashes for the example mentioned above:

- LayerZero Scan: https://layerzeroscan.com/106/address/0xe6772d0b85756d1af98ddfc61c5339e10d1b6eff/message/109/address/0x5285413ea82ac98a220dd65405c91d735f4133d8/nonce/1
- Tenderly stack trace of the sending transaction hash: https://dashboard.tenderly.co/tx/avalanche-mainnet/0xe54894bd

The owner will be subjected to a higher liquidation risk due to use of more collateral and higher borrowing.

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token-audit/blob/main/contracts/governance/twTAP.sol#L278-L282


# Vulnerability details

## Proof of Concept 
Every time new twTAP participant is joing a pool, new magnitude for twTAP holder is computed by `computeMagnitude`.

```solidity
        uint256 magnitude = computeMagnitude(_duration, pool.cumulative); //@audit - twAML magnitude
```

It will update pool's cumulative and average magnitude.

As average magnitude should be mathematical average of all participant's magnitude, it should be updated as following.

- cumulative magnitude += new magnitude;
- average magnitude = cumulative magnitude / participants;

But implementation is different.

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token-audit/blob/main/contracts/governance/twTAP.sol#L278-L282
```solidity
            pool.totalParticipants++; // Save participation
            pool.averageMagnitude =
                (pool.averageMagnitude + magnitude) /
                pool.totalParticipants; // compute new average magnitude 
                // @audit - wrong calculation of average, should be pool.cumulative
```

## Impact
Pool's average magnitude will get smaller and smaller as the number of participants grows. It will affect twTAP price.

## Recommendation
Should replace `pool.averageMagnitude + magnitude` with `pool.averageMagnitude + magnitude`.

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token-audit/blob/main/contracts/governance/twTAP.sol#L278-L282
```solidity
            pool.totalParticipants++; // Save participation
            pool.averageMagnitude =
-               (pool.averageMagnitude + magnitude) /
+               (pool.cumulative + magnitude) /
                pool.totalParticipants; // compute new average magnitude 
                // @audit - wrong calculation of average, should be pool.cumulative
```


## Assessed type

Math

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token-audit/blob/59749be5bc2286f0bdbf59d7ddc258ddafd49a9f/contracts/governance/twTAP.sol#L111


# Vulnerability details


`twTAP` is a omnichain NFT (ONFT721) that will be deployed on all supported chains.

However, there are no access control for operations meant for execution on the host chain only, such as `participate()`, which mints `twTAP`. 

The implication of not restricting `participate()` to host chain is that an attacker can lock `TAP` and participate on other chain to mint `twTAP` with a tokenId that does not exist on the host chain yet. The attacker can then send that `twTAP` to the host chain using the inherited `sendFrom()`, to permanently freeze the `twTAP` contract as `participate()` will fail when attempting to mint an existing `tokenId`.

It is important to restrict minting to the host chain so that `mintedTWTap` (which keeps track of last minted tokenId) is only incremented at one chain, to prevent duplicate tokenId. That is because the `twTAP` contracts on each chain have their own `mintedTWTap` variable and there is no mechanism to sync them.

In `TwTAP`, there are no modifiers or checks to ensure `participte()` can only be called on the host chain. So we can use it to mint a `twTAP` on a non-host chain.

## Proof of Concept
According to the Stargate's documentation on ["How to swap"](https://stargateprotocol.gitbook.io/stargate/developers/how-to-swap),

# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/markets/bigBang/BigBang.sol#L192


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
DOS of BigBang's functions (such as repay, liquidate, ...) when total debt of BigBang below `debtStartPoint`
## Proof of concept
```solidity=
function getDebtRate() public view returns (uint256) {
    if (_isEthMarket) return penrose.bigBangEthDebtRate(); // default 0.5%
    if (totalBorrow.elastic == 0) return minDebtRate;

    uint256 _ethMarketTotalDebt = BigBang(penrose.bigBangEthMarket())
        .getTotalDebt();
    uint256 _currentDebt = totalBorrow.elastic;
    uint256 _maxDebtPoint = (_ethMarketTotalDebt *
        debtRateAgainstEthMarket) / 1e18;

    if (_currentDebt >= _maxDebtPoint) return maxDebtRate;

    uint256 debtPercentage = ((_currentDebt - debtStartPoint) *
        DEBT_PRECISION) / (_maxDebtPoint - debtStartPoint);
    ...
}
```
There is no check if `_currentDebt` is below `debtStartPoint`. Therefore, if `totalBorrow.elastic` (total debt of BigBang) is below `debtStartPoint`, this function will be reverted due to underflow. This function is triggered by `accrue` function, so BigBang market will be DOS in this case.
## Tool used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add the check if `_currentDebt` is below `debtStartPoint`:
```solidity=
if (_currentDebt <= debtStartPoint) return minDebtRate;
```


## Assessed type

DoS

Function `_isSolvent` in `Market` contract use conversion from share to amount of yieldBox.
```solidity=
yieldBox.toAmount(
    collateralId,
    collateralShare *
        (EXCHANGE_RATE_PRECISION / FEE_PRECISION) *

    false
)

It will trigger `_toAmount` function in `YieldBoxRebase` contract
```solidity=
function _toAmount(
    uint256 share,
    uint256 totalShares_,
    uint256 totalAmount,
    bool roundUp
) internal pure returns (uint256 amount) {
    totalAmount++;
    totalShares_ += 1e8;

    amount = (share * totalAmount) / totalShares_;

    if (roundUp && (amount * totalShares_) / totalAmount < share) {

Users were unable to purchase their deserved amount of TAPs

During each `epoch` and for a specific `sglAssetID`, there is a fixed amount of TAP tokens that will be minted and stored in the STORAGE mapping `singularityGauges[epoch][sglAssetID]`. Users have the option to purchase these TAP tokens by first calling the function `TapiocaOptionBroker.participate()` and then executing `TapiocaOptionBroker.exerciseOption()` before the position expires to buy TAPs at a discounted price. The amount of TAP tokens that a user can purchase with each position can be calculated using the formula:

```
eligibleTapAmount = position.amount * gaugeTotalForEpoch / totalPoolDeposited

- position.amount: The locked amount of the position in `sglAssetId`.

# Vulnerability details

Singularity has a public function `multiHopBuyCollateral` that is designed to allow users to lever up by borrowing more assets and buying collateral with it across chains. Notably, the function allows an arbitrary `address from`, `uint256 collateralAmount` and `uint256 borrowAmount`.

To prevent abuse, the function has the following checks:
- `solvent(from)`
- `_allowedBorrow(from, collateralShare)`
  - where `collateralShare` is calculated from input `collateralAmount` and `yieldBox.toShare()`

In actuality, the `_allowedBorrow(from, collateralShare)` check can bypassed by providing input `collateralAmount = 0`. Notably, the `borrowAmount` input is not checked for any user allowances for `msg.sender` and will cause side effects.

```js

    // .. snip ..
    uint256 collateralShare = yieldBox.toShare(
        collateralId,
        collateralAmount,
        false
    );
    _allowedBorrow(from, collateralShare); // @audit-issue Can pass this with collateralAmount = 0
    // .. snip ..
}
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/bcf61f79464cfdc0484aa272f9f6e28d5de36a8f/contracts/tOFT/BaseTOFT.sol#L539-L545

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Exercise option cross chain message in the `(m)TapiocaOFT` will always revert in the destination, but works in the source chain, where it debits the funds from users. Thus, these funds will not be credited in the destination and are forever lost.

## Proof of Concept
In the `BaseTOFT`, if the packet from the received cross chain message in `lzReceive()` is of type `PT_TAP_EXERCISE`, it delegate calls to the `BaseTOFTOptionsModule`:

```solidity
function _nonblockingLzReceive(
    uint16 _srcChainId,
    bytes memory _srcAddress,
    uint64 _nonce,
    bytes memory _payload
) internal virtual override {
    uint256 packetType = _payload.toUint256(0);
    ...
    } else if (packetType == PT_TAP_EXERCISE) {
        _executeOnDestination(
            Module.Options,
            abi.encodeWithSelector(
                BaseTOFTOptionsModule.exercise.selector,
                _srcChainId,
                _srcAddress,
                _nonce,
                _payload
            ),
            _srcChainId,
            _srcAddress,
            _nonce,
            _payload
        );
    ...
```

In the `BaseTOFTOptionsModule`, the `exercise()` function is declared as:
```solidity
function exercise(
    address module,
    uint16 _srcChainId,
    bytes memory _srcAddress,
    uint64 _nonce,
    bytes memory _payload
) public {
    ...
}
```
Notice that the `address module` argument is specified in the `exercise()` function declaration, but not in the `_nonBlockingLzReceive()` call to it. This will make the message always revert because it fails when decoding the arguments to the function call, due to the extra `address module` argument.

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token-audit/blob/59749be5bc2286f0bdbf59d7ddc258ddafd49a9f/contracts/options/TapiocaOptionBroker.sol#L426-L427
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token-audit/blob/59749be5bc2286f0bdbf59d7ddc258ddafd49a9f/contracts/tokens/TapOFT.sol#L201


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Users will not get emitted ```TAP``` tokens when there are emissions because zero TAP will be emitted leading to a loss of funds for users and the protocol.

## Proof of Concept
when setting a newEpoch by calling ```newEpoch(...)``` a call is made to ```emitForWeek(..)``` in the ```TapOFT.sol``` to calculate the the emission for the week. However, the logic in the function returns 0 if there is an emission of TAP in the current week, ```(emission > 0)```. 
```
    function newEpoch() external {
        
        ...
        uint256 epochTAP = tapOFT.emitForWeek();
        _emitToGauges(epochTAP);

        ...
    }
```
This means that whenever there is an emission, the ```epochTAP is zero and as such 0 is retured indicating TAP is not emitted for the week.

```
    function emitForWeek() external notPaused returns (uint256) {
        ...

        if (emissionForWeek[week] > 0) return 0;

        /...

        emit Emitted(week, emission);

        ...
    }
```


## Tools Used
Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Adjust the logic in the ```emitForWeek(..)``` function to be  ```==``` instead of ```>``` as shown below
```
    function emitForWeek() external notPaused returns (uint256) {
        ...

        if (emissionForWeek[week] == 0) return 0;

        /...

        emit Emitted(week, emission);

        ...
    }
```

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
In `BigBang.sol`, the contract has an initializer function that can be called only once, yet the has no authorization checks and it's left open for anyone to call. This means a front runner can initialize the contract with their chosen data parameters. An attacker can add parameters which allows them to steal collateral from users.

## Proof of Concept
An example of how modified parameters can be used to steal users' funds:

1) Contract init is front run with a custom oracle address
2) The custom oracle is a contract whose owner can manipulate oracle prices at will
3) Users will then borrow as usual, oracle will for now work as intended
4) Eventually the attacker will then set the price of the collateral to near zero
5) Finally, this attacker will liquidate as many users as possible

## Tools Used
Manual code reading

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Add an `onlyOwner` modifier in the linked code line.

```
    function init(bytes calldata data) external onlyOwner onlyOnce {
```

`SGLCommon.sol` contains a function `_getInterestRate()` which calculates the current interest rate. issues.title: `computeMinWeight` computes the minimum weight incorrectly by a factor of 10
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token-audit/blob/59749be5bc2286f0bdbf59d7ddc258ddafd49a9f/contracts/twAML.sol#L120


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Logical error causes minimum voting weight to be 10x lower than intended.

## Proof of Concept
In `twTAP.participate`, we compute whether the `_amount` to participate with is sufficient to have voting power.

```solidity
// Calculate twAML voting weight
bool hasVotingPower = _amount >=
	computeMinWeight(pool.totalDeposited, MIN_WEIGHT_FACTOR);
```

We pass a value of 10 bps, or 0.1% (as correctly documented) as the `_minWeightFactor`.

```solidity
uint256 constant MIN_WEIGHT_FACTOR = 10; // In BPS, 0.1%
```

The problem lies in `computeMinWeight`, wherein we multiply the `_totalWeight` by the `_minWeightFactor`, but then divide by 1e4 instead of 1e5 which would actually represent 10000 bps or 100%. As a result, the minimum weight return is 10x lower than the intended minimum weight.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`computeMinWeight` should divide by 1e5 rather than 1e4 to correctly use the bps value of `_minWeightFactor`.

Other

`liquidationMultiplier` set as 10x the intended amount leads to 10x the intended amount being liquidated.

// _updateBorrowAndCollateralShare

);
if (collateralShare > userCollateralShare[user]) {
	collateralShare = userCollateralShare[user];
}
userCollateralShare[user] -= collateralShare;
```

# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/markets/Market.sol#L75


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`borrowOpeningFee` is 10x greater than intended, thereby charging users 10x as much as intended to open a borrow position.

## Proof of Concept
`borrowOpeningFee` is intended to be set as 0.05% or 5 bps but is actually set as 0.5% or 50 bps.

```solidity
uint256 public borrowOpeningFee = 50; //0.05%
```

As a result, users are charged a fee of 10x the intended amount.

```solidity
uint256 feeAmount = (amount * borrowOpeningFee) / FEE_PRECISION; // A flat % fee is charged for any borrow
```

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`borrowOpeningFee` should be set as `5`.


## Assessed type

Other

issues.title: Reentrancy in `USDO.flashLoan()`, enabling an attacker to borrow unlimited USDO exceeding the max borrow limit
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/usd0/USDO.sol#L81-L97


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

Due to an reentrancy attack vector, an attacker can flashLoan an unlimited amount of USDO. For example the attacker can create a malicious contract as the `receiver`, to execute the attack via the `onFlashLoan` callback (line 94 USDO.sol).

The exploit works because `USDO.flashLoan()` is missing a reentrancy protection (modifier). 

As a result an unlimited amount of USDO can be borrowed by an attacker via the flashLoan exploit described above.

## Proof of Concept

Here is a POC that shows an exploit:

https://gist.github.com/zzzitron/a121bc1ba8cc947d927d4629a90f7991

To run the exploit add this malicious contract into the contracts folder:

https://gist.github.com/zzzitron/8de3be7ddf674cc19a6272b59cfccde1


## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Consider adding some reentrancy protection modifier to `USDO.flashLoan()`.





## Assessed type

Reentrancy

issues.title: [MF02] `BaseTOFT.sol`: `_wrap` allowance checked but not reduced
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/bcf61f79464cfdc0484aa272f9f6e28d5de36a8f/contracts/tOFT/BaseTOFT.sol#L348-L361


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The function `_wrap` in `BaseTOFT.sol` checks that the `msg.sender` has enough allowance to wrap the amount of tokens it is trying to wrap. This is done in the following snippet:

```solidity
if (_fromAddress != msg.sender) {
    require(
        allowance(_fromAddress, msg.sender) >= _amount,
        "TOFT_allowed"
    );
}
IERC20(erc20).safeTransferFrom(_fromAddress, address(this), _amount);
_mint(_toAddress, _amount);
```

The issue is that although the allowance is checked, it isnt reduced. Thus a msg.sender with an allowance of 1 ether can wrap 1000 ether as long as they send the wrap transaction in 100 different calls.

Since this defeats the purpose of having the allowance as a fixed amount, this is classified as a medium issue.

## Proof of Concept

The bug can be observed by doing the following steps.

1. User gives allowance of 1 ether to some wallet Alice.
2. Alice wraps 1 ether. Alice repeats the same operation sending 1 ether at a time.
3. Since the allowance is never reduced, Alice can wrap as much ether in the User's name as possible.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Decrement the allowance by the `amount` being wrapped.



## Assessed type

Math

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The function `sendToStrategy` is used to send tokens cross-chain to a yieldbox. this can be done to send tokens to any user's yieldbox, regardless of allowances. The function takes the argument `to`, which define target's address.

`BaseTOFT.sol`:`sendToStrategy` is called by the attacker with a `to` address of the target. This function calls the `sendToStrategy` function in the strategy module.

This function packs some data and sends it forward to the lz endpoint. Point to note, is that no approval check is done for the `msg.sender` of this whole setup yet. The victim's `to` address is passed in the third field.

```solidity
bytes memory lzPayload = abi.encode(
    PT_YB_SEND_STRAT,
    LzLib.addressToBytes32(_from),
    toAddress,
    amount,
    share,
    assetId,
    options.zroPaymentAddress
);
// lzsend(...)
```

    uint256 share,

) = abi.decode(

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/bcf61f79464cfdc0484aa272f9f6e28d5de36a8f/contracts/tOFT/modules/BaseTOFTLeverageModule.sol#L195-L200
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/bcf61f79464cfdc0484aa272f9f6e28d5de36a8f/contracts/tOFT/modules/BaseTOFTMarketModule.sol#L170-L175
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/bcf61f79464cfdc0484aa272f9f6e28d5de36a8f/contracts/tOFT/modules/BaseTOFTOptionsModule.sol#L202-L212
https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/bcf61f79464cfdc0484aa272f9f6e28d5de36a8f/contracts/tOFT/modules/BaseTOFTStrategyModule.sol#L163-L168


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The TapiocaOFT and mTapiocaOFT contracts handle cross chain operations. Incase of failure, some of these cross chain operations have code for error-handling, where the intention is to send the raw assets to an address in case the loan/borrow/leverage functionality does not go through. An example can be seen here, taken from the market module's `borrow` function.

```solidity
(bool success, bytes memory reason) = module.delegatecall(
    abi.encodeWithSelector(
        this.borrowInternal.selector,
        _to,
        borrowParams,
        withdrawParams,
        approvals
    )
);

if (!success) {
    if (balanceAfter - balanceBefore >= borrowParams.amount) {
        IERC20(address(this)).safeTransfer(_from, borrowParams.amount);
    }
    revert(_getRevertMsg(reason)); //forward revert because it's handled by the main executor
}
```

Here, first the internal function `borrowInternal` is called. In case that call fails, the second block of code is there to transfer the raw assets to the owner. This second clause is however incorrectly implemented. This is because while the inner if statement checks if the balance in the contract has increased for a potential refund, the `revert` statement outside is always executed, negating the refund. Thus the refund never actually happens, and the whole transaction is reverted.

issues.title: [HF01] TapiocaOFT and mTapiocaOFT tokens in old contract wallets can be hijacked
issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapiocaz-audit/blob/bcf61f79464cfdc0484aa272f9f6e28d5de36a8f/contracts/tOFT/BaseTOFT.sol#L450-L571


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

TapiocaOFT and mTapiocaOFT tokens have multichain functionality, which allows users to send interact with as well as run operations on other chains. An example is the `retrieveFromStrategy` function, which allows a user to withdraw wrapped tokens form the yieldbox on some other chain and then transfer them back out to their current chain. This basically implements a "pulling" action on the tokens, and users are thus allowed to "pull" tokens from other chains to their current one. The main issue is that the protocol makes the inherent assumption that the same wallet address on both chains are owned by the same person. While this is true for EOA wallets, this is not true for smart contract wallets such as Gnosis safe wallets.

Gnosis safe wallets and other similar contract wallets are deployed as beacon proxies from a central wallet factory. Older versions of the beacon proxy were generated by the `ProxyFactory` contract, which used the `create` opcode instead of `create2`. thus the wallet addresses generated were only a function of the factory contract address and the nonce. Thus user A can deploy a contract wallet on chain 1, and a different user B can deploy a wallet with the same address on chain 2 as long as they use the same nonce, and the factory was deployed by gnosis to the same addresses. This was the case for the first Wintermute incident, where Wintermute had sent the address of their gnosis wallet on mainnet to the Optimism team, who were expecting an address on the Optimism chain. After the tokens were transferred on the optimism chain, an attacker was able to create lots of wallets until they hit the exact nonce and thus got control of the exact wallet address on the optimism chain. # Vulnerability details

## Impact

As an example, when calling `BigBang.liquidate()` the tx potentially fails, because the subsequent call to `Market.updateExchangeRate` (BigBang.sol line 316) can face a revert condition on line 344 in Market.sol.

In `Market.updateExchangeRate()` a revert is triggered if `rate` is not bigger than 0 - see line 344 in Market.sol.

Liquidations should never fail and instead use the old exchange rate - see BigBang.sol line 315 comment:
> // Oracle can fail but we still need to allow liquidations

But the liquidation transaction can potentially fail when trying to fetch the new exchange rate via `Market.updateExchangeRate()` as shown above.

This issue applies for all markets (Singularity, BigBang) since the revert during the liquidation happens in the Market.sol contract from which all markets inherit.

Because of this issue user's collateral values may fall below their debt values, without being able to liquidate them, pushing the protocol into insolvency.

This is classified as high risk because liquidation is an essential functionality of the protocol.

## Proof of Concept

Here is a POC that shows that a liquidation tx reverts according to the issue described above:

https://gist.github.com/zzzitron/90206267434a90990ff2ee12e7deebb0

## Tools Used

Manual review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Instead of reverting on line 344 in Market.sol when fetching the exchange rate, consider to return the old rate instead, so that the liquidation can be executed successfully.


## Assessed type

Other

# Vulnerability details

## Impact

TapOFT tokens have multichain functionality, which allows users to send interact with as well as run operations on other chains. An example is the `claimRewards` function, which allows a user to claim rewards on a destination and chain transfer them back out to their current chain. This basically implements a "pulling" action on the reward tokens, and users are thus allowed to "pull" tokens from other chains to their current one. The main issue is that the protocol makes the inherent assumption that the same wallet address on both chains are owned by the same person. While this is true for EOA wallets, this is not true for smart contract wallets such as Gnosis safe wallets.

Gnosis safe wallets and other similar contract wallets are deployed as beacon proxies from a central wallet factory. Older versions of the beacon proxy were generated by the `ProxyFactory` contract, which used the `create` opcode instead of `create2`. thus the wallet adresses generated were only a function of the factory contract address and the nonce. Thus user A can deploy a contract wallet on chain 1, and a different user B can deploy a wallet with the same address on chain 2 as long as they use the same nonce, and the factory was deployed by gnosis to the same addresses. This was the case for the first Wintermute incident, where Wintermute had sent the address of their gnosis wallet on mainnet to the Optimism team, who were expecting an address on the Optimism chain. After the tokens were transferred on the optimism chain, an attacker was able to create lots of wallets until they hit the exact nonce and thus got control of the exact wallet address on the optimism chain. issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/markets/bigBang/BigBang.sol#L604-L606


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

The function `liquidate` in `BigbBang.sol` is used to liquidate positions with bad health. This function does a swap of the user's collateral assets to pay off their borrowed tokens. This function also takes in a bytes32 in the parameter `collateralToAssetSwapData` which it passes on to the DEX being used for the swap. This is seen in the following snippet in function `_liquidateUser`.

```solidity
if (dexData.length > 0) {
    minAssetAmount = abi.decode(dexData, (uint256));
}
```

Where `_dexData` is the passed input from the liquidator. The `minAssetAmount` is passed to the DEX wrapper and is the minimum amount of loan tokens that the collateral tokens must be swapped for. This is a check put in place to protect users from sandwich attacks and price manipulation, by setting a bound for the worst price the user is willing to pay.

In this case however, the `liquidate` function only takes one input for the `collateralToAssetSwapData` parameter. The liquidation targets however are taken as an array and the function is capable of handling multiple liquidations. Thus the same `collateralToAssetSwapData` is re-used for each liquidation. The problem with this approach is that the liquidated amounts can be different for different liquidation targets. Thus the same `minAssetAmount` is used for all swap operations. If the minimum amount is too high, then the swaps will revert, reverting the whole liquidation call. Therefore the minamount must be set to the minimum possible amount for the smallest liquidation among all liquidation targets. This essentially removes all slippage protection from the liquidator, and can force the liquidator to take large losses since the min amount has to be artificially low for the transaction to pass through.

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/markets/bigBang/BigBang.sol#L149


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Incorrectly set state var leads to liquidation reverting, compromising economic guarantees of the protocol.

## Proof of Concept
In both BigBang and Singularity, `protocolFee` is set as 100% or 10000 bps when it's intended to be set as 10% or 1000 bps.

```solidity
protocolFee = 10000; // 10%
```

As a result, during liquidation, in `_extractLiquidationFees` it transfers 100% of the remaining tokens available to the `feeTo` address, then also attempts to transfer tokens to msg.sender.

```solidity
function _extractLiquidationFees(
	uint256 returnedShare,
	uint256 borrowShare,
	uint256 callerReward
) private returns (uint256 feeShare, uint256 callerShare) {
	uint256 extraShare = returnedShare - borrowShare;
	feeShare = (extraShare * protocolFee) / FEE_PRECISION; // x% of profit goes to fee.
	callerShare = (extraShare * callerReward) / FEE_PRECISION; //  y%  of profit goes to caller.

	yieldBox.transfer(address(this), penrose.feeTo(), assetId, feeShare);
	yieldBox.transfer(address(this), msg.sender, assetId, callerShare);
}
```

Of course, since we're trying to send >100% of the available tokens, the function reverts. With liquidation being fundamental to the system's economic guarantees, this failure allows users to remain insolvent, potentially leading to total protocol insolvency.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`protocolFee` should be set as `1000`.


## Assessed type

DoS

# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-bar-audit/blob/2286f80f928f41c8bc189d0657d74ba83286c668/contracts/usd0/modules/USDOOptionsModule.sol#L24-L56


# Vulnerability details

## Impact

UDSO tokens have multichain functionality, which allows users to send as well as receive USDO tokens from one chain to another. An example is the `triggerSendFrom` function, which allows a user to transfer from some source chain to their current chain. This basically implements a "pulling" action on the token, and users are thus allowed to "pull" tokens from other chains to their current one. The main issue is that the protocol makes the inherent assumption that the same wallet address on both chains are owned by the same person. While this is true for EOA wallets, this is not true for smart contract wallets such as Gnosis safe wallets.

Gnosis safe wallets and other similar contract wallets are deployed as beacon proxies from a central wallet factory. Older versions of the beacon proxy were generated by the `ProxyFactory` contract, which used the `create` opcode instead of `create2`. thus the wallet adresses generated were only a function of the factory contract address and the nonce. Thus user A can deploy a contract wallet on chain 1, and a different user B can deploy a wallet with the same address on chain 2 as long as they use the same nonce, and the factory was deployed by gnosis to the same addresses. This was the case for the first Wintermute incident, where Wintermute had sent the address of their gnosis wallet on mainnet to the Optimism team, who were expecting an address on the Optimism chain. After the tokens were transferred on the optimism chain, an attacker was able to create lots of wallets until they hit the exact nonce and thus got control of the exact wallet address on the optimism chain. More details about the incident can be found on the rekt leaderboard [here](https://rekt.news/wintermute-rekt/).

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
Caller receives 10x the intended amount of the caller liquidation fee due to incorrect state var.

## Proof of Concept
In Singularity, the `callerFee` is set as 10% or 1000 bps when it is intended to be set as 1% or 100 bps.

```solidity
callerFee = 1000; // 1%
```

As a result, during liquidation when we calculate the share to be paid to the caller, that amount is calculated as 10% of the remaining tokens available from the liquidation.

```solidity
uint256 returnedShare = yieldBox.balanceOf(address(this), assetId) -
	uint256(totalAsset.elastic);
uint256 extraShare = returnedShare - allBorrowShare;
// @audit: caller should get 1% of fee but actually gets 10%
uint256 callerShare = (extraShare * callerFee) / FEE_PRECISION; // 1% goes to caller
```

This causes the caller to receive 10x the intended amount.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
`callerFee` should be set as `100`.

The function `emergencyWithdraw` in the lido strategy contract is used to withdraw all tokens by exchanging them on the curve steth-eth pool. The function calls the `removeLiquidityWeth` function which removes the actual liquidity and passes the parameter `minAmount` which represents the minimum output amount expected. The `minAmount` is however calculated incorrectly.

All the other strategies defined minimum amount as 99.5% of the calculated amount. However in this case, the amount is calculated to be 0.5% instead of 99.5% as shown.

```solidity
uint256 minAmount = (toWithdraw * 50) / 10_000; //0.5%
```

Since this mistake removes slippage protection on a very large value (the entire assets managed by that strategy), this is classified as a high severity issue.

## Proof of Concept

The bug is obvious since the `minamount` evaluates to 0.5% of the calculated amount.

## Tools Used

Manual Review

## Recommended Mitigation Steps

Correct the expression to calculate the minimum amount correctly, which should be 99.5%, as shown below.

```solidity
uint256 minAmount = toWithdraw - (toWithdraw * 50) / 10_000;
```

Math

# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`LidoEthStrategy.emergencyWithdraw` execution can lead to up to 99.5% of the strategy balance to be taken by sandwich bots.

## Proof of Concept
`LidoEthStrategy.emergencyWithdraw` makes the mistake of passing a `minAmount` to receive of just 0.5% of the contract STETH balance.

```solidity
function emergencyWithdraw() external onlyOwner returns (uint256 result) {
	compound("");

	uint256 toWithdraw = stEth.balanceOf(address(this));
	uint256 minAmount = (toWithdraw * 50) / 10_000; //0.5% @audit: oops
	result = curveStEthPool.exchange(1, 0, toWithdraw, minAmount);

	INative(address(wrappedNative)).deposit{value: result}();
}
```

As a result, any time `emergencyWithdraw` is called, a sandwich bot will likely sandwich the transaction, leaving the strategy with as little as 0.5% of the balance they ought to receive.

## Recommended Mitigation Steps
Presumably, the intended `minAmount` to provide is 99.5% and should thus be used instead. Although it's important to also consider the discrepancy in exchange rate between ETH<>STETH.

# Vulnerability details

# Vulnerability details
The AaveStrategy contract is designed to:
1. Receive depositor's ERC20 tokens from yieldBox
2. Deposit those tokens into an AAVE lending pool
3. Allow anyone to call `compound()`, which:
    a. Claims AAVE rewards from the `incentivesController`
    b. Claims staking rewards from the `stakingRewardToken` (stkAAVE)
    c. Redeeming staking rewards is only possible within a certain cooldown window that is set by AAVE governance. The function resets the cooldown if either 12 days have passed since the cooldown was last initiated, or if the strategy has a stakedRewardToken balance
    d. Swaps any received `rewardToken` ($AAVE) for `wrappedNative`
    e. Deposits the `wrappedNative` received in the swap into the lending pool

issues.body:
# Lines of code

https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token-audit/blob/59749be5bc2286f0bdbf59d7ddc258ddafd49a9f/contracts/options/oTAP.sol#L115-L123


# Vulnerability details

## Impact
`burn` function does not check if the token is actually owned by the caller. This means that an attacker could call the burn function with a token ID that they do not own, and the contract would burn the token.

## Proof of Concept

**[burn](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tap-token-audit/blob/59749be5bc2286f0bdbf59d7ddc258ddafd49a9f/contracts/options/oTAP.sol#L115-L123) function**
```solidity
function burn(uint256 _tokenId) external {
    require(
        _isApprovedOrOwner(msg.sender, _tokenId),
        "OTAP: only approved or owner"
    );
    _burn(_tokenId);

    emit Burn(msg.sender, _tokenId, options[_tokenId]);
}
```
There will be a chance of reentrancy vulnerability caused by the order of operations in the `burn` function. The `_burn` function, which removes the token from the owner's account and modifies the contract state, is called before the `require` statement that checks if the caller is the owner or an approved address. This sequence of operations creates a window of opportunity for reentrancy attacks.

Here's an exploit scenario that demonstrates how the reentrancy vulnerability can be abused:

1. A malicious external contract, let's call it "Attacker," calls the `burn` function of the OTAP contract with the token ID of an OTAP token it doesn't own.

2. The `burn` function is executed, and the `_burn` function is called, which removes the OTAP token from the owner's account and modifies the contract state.

3. Before the `require` statement is reached, the `Attacker` contract's fallback function is triggered as part of the reentrancy attack.

4. The `Attacker` contract's fallback function calls the `burn` function again, passing the token ID of another OTAP token that belongs to a legitimate user.
